newsitem.title: USA: Bombing survivor opposes McVeigh death sentence.
newsitem.headline: Bombing survivor opposes McVeigh death sentence.

text.p: One survivor of the Oklahoma City explosion declared his opposition in an interview published Thursday to a death penalty for convicted bomber Timothy McVeigh.

Bennie Evans, 42, who was severely injured while working as a supervisor in an Army recruiting office at the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building, spoke out in an interview with the Anchorage Daily News against sentencing McVeigh to death.

"Life is so valuable, even his," Evans, a Gulf War veteran like McVeigh, told the newspaper, which carried a Page One article about him. "His crime was caused by hate and killing him would nurture the hate. There's too much hate in our society. And this hate has to stop somewhere."

Evans also said sentencing McVeigh to death could make it more difficult to learn about any possible co-conspirators. If he gets a life sentence instead, "later on, he might talk about the others," Evans said.
"If he dies, he might become a martyr to whoever these people are, these people who knew there were kids in that building. McVeigh killed 168 people, yes, but he couldn't have done it by himself."

The Daily News account said that after the bombing, Evans and his wife, Rhonda, now a staff sergeant at Anchorage's Fort Richardson Army Base, sought a transfer to Alaska so they could be as far away as possible from the site of the blast.

Now retired from the Army, Evans is studying business at the University of Alaska Anchorage. His back and legs were injured by the blast and he was confined for a time to a wheelchair, the Daily News said.
